item.title: By: Carl Abbott
item.dc:creator: Carl Abbott
item.description:
Yes, this shows how profoundly circumstances <sup>1</sup> mold culture, and every facet of that culture. One of the main errors we make in judgment is the overwhelming tendency to pick and choose elements of culture as being the cause behind aspects we abhor. We fail to see particular problems as actually symptoms of deeper causes, i.e., <a href="https://centertao.local/blog/2010/11/22/a-symptoms-point-of-view/" rel="nofollow">Symptoms Point Of View</a>. I imagine the pressing need for cognitive closure (NFCC) drives us to hasty and shallow conclusions... facts be damned... See <a href="https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Closure_%28psychology%29" rel="nofollow">Closure (psychology)</a>.
<sup>1</sup> Naturally, circumstances include our instinctive needs and fears (our biology) as they express themselves through the cultural paradigm in which we are conditioned. It can easily become a bit of a vicious circle.

item.title: By: Dian Reed
item.dc:creator: Dian Reed
item.description: This quote really made an impression on me: "Fighting is dangerous—someone might get killed." How different from our own culture's Dulce et decorum est pro patria mori--which promotes dying for glory. I suppose the different attitudes are based on population size and the abundance or scarcity of food. If every single person is critical to the survival of the others, each person is a commodity too valuable to squander. Makes me think of traditional New Guinea tribes, where boys are raised specifically to be warriors and killing the enemy (anyone "not us") is the equivalent of an Olympic sport. The abundance of food leads to higher populations and the expendability of warriors. Reminds me of chapter 69.
